title: Pritam Said He Wanted to Explore the Roads Unexplored. The First Road Led Away From a ₹500-Crore Epic.
excerpt: Amit Trivedi steps into the Shivaji Maharaj biopic after Bollywood's most bankable composer announced his creative sabbatical — and it might be the most interesting thing to happen to Hindi film music all year
body:
Pritam Chakraborty turned fifty-five on June 14, and what should have been a routine celebrity birthday post became something else entirely. On Instagram, alongside a series of black-and-white photographs that looked like they belonged in a Zurich gallery, the man who scored the soundtrack to an entire generation's love life wrote this: "I have decided to gift myself a few years to live life differently. To catch up on what I've missed. Mainstream is a great ride. But I've always been more curious about the roads unexplored."

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=NW6UlyUBz10</youtube>

The internet did what the internet does — panicked. First Arijit Singh announced he was stepping back from playback singing. Now Pritam? Bollywood's two most bankable musical pillars were apparently heading for the exits at the same time, and social media treated it like the industry's version of a market crash.

A source close to Pritam later told *Hindustan Times* that no, the composer was not leaving the music industry. He would complete his existing commitments — a slate that still includes *Golmaal 5*, *Bhagam Bhag 2*, and *Haiwaan* — before pivoting to independent and experimental work that has been collecting dust on his back burner for years. Not a retirement, then. A recalibration. But the first domino has already fallen.

## The First Departure

On July 1, the makers of *The Pride of Bharat: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj* confirmed what industry circles had been whispering: Pritam is out, and National Award-winning composer Amit Trivedi is in. The two-part historical epic, starring Rishab Shetty as the Maratha warrior king, is being mounted on a reported budget north of ₹500 crore — making it one of the most expensive Indian films ever produced. Losing your composer on a project of this scale is not a minor personnel shuffle. It is a creative reset.

Trivedi's appointment makes a certain poetic sense. Where Pritam's genius has always been populist — the hummable hook, the wedding-ready anthem, the chorus that 1.4 billion people can sing after one listen — Trivedi operates closer to the earth. His best work (*Dev D*, *Queen*, *Lootera*, *Sacred Games*) draws from folk traditions, classical ragas, and the kind of controlled chaos that sounds effortless and is anything but. For a film about a warrior king who built an empire from scratch, you want music that feels rooted rather than radio-ready.

The rest of the creative team remains intact. Prasoon Joshi, the National Award-winning lyricist who has been attached since the project's inception, will continue writing the songs. Director Sandeep Singh is aiming for principal photography later this year, with the first chapter tentatively slated for 2028 and the second for 2029. The cast — Rishab Shetty, Arjun Rampal, Vivek Oberoi — is already locked. This is a ship that has been built and is ready to sail; it just needed a new navigator for the music.

## What Pritam Leaves Behind

It is difficult to overstate what Pritam has meant to Bollywood over the last two decades. *Jab We Met* plays at every NRI wedding reception between New Jersey and Southall. *Barfi* made people cry in languages the film was not even made in. *Ae Dil Hai Mushkil*, *Brahmāstra*, the *Cocktail* soundtrack — his discography reads like a map of how the Indian diaspora has experienced heartbreak, celebration, and homesickness through cinema.

When a composer of that stature steps back — even partially, even temporarily — it creates a vacuum that no single replacement can fill. Amit Trivedi is brilliant, but he is a different kind of brilliant. The question is whether Bollywood's commercial machine, addicted to Pritam's particular brand of earworm, can adapt to the shift.

## The Bigger Question

Between Pritam's recalibration and Arijit Singh's retreat from playback singing, Bollywood's musical establishment is going through something that resembles, if not a crisis, then at least an uncomfortable adolescence. The industry's two most reliable hit-makers are pulling away from the mainstream just as film budgets are ballooning and the pressure to deliver pan-India chart-toppers has never been higher.

For the diaspora audience — the ones who grew up humming "*Tum Se Hi*" in minivans on the Garden State Parkway, who play "*Channa Mereya*" at every mehendi — this is not just an industry story. It is the slow turning of a musical era that soundtracked your life abroad. What comes next might be better, might be worse, but it will certainly be different.

Amit Trivedi composing for a ₹500 crore Shivaji Maharaj epic is a good place for that difference to start.
author: Diaspora Desk
